scenes.heading: Kubernetes Fundamentals
scenes.narration: Kubernetes orchestrates containers at scale, and it starts with three core building blocks: pods, deployments, and services.

scenes.heading: The three core objects
bullets: Pod: the smallest deployable unit, one or more containers
Deployment: manages replicas and rolling updates
Service: a stable network endpoint for pods
Labels and selectors tie them all together
scenes.narration: A pod is the smallest unit Kubernetes schedules, wrapping one or more tightly coupled containers. A deployment sits above pods, managing how many replicas run and rolling out new versions safely. A service provides a stable network address so clients can reach pods even as they come and go. Labels and selectors are the glue that lets these objects find each other.

scenes.heading: How a request reaches your pod
scenes.narration: A client sends its request to the service, which acts as a stable front door. The service uses label selectors to find the healthy pods behind it. It then load-balances the traffic across those pods, and finally a chosen pod handles the request. This indirection is what makes pods disposable and replaceable.

scenes.heading: A Deployment manifest
scenes.code:
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: etl-worker
spec:
  replicas: 3
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: etl-worker
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: etl-worker
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: worker
          image: myrepo/etl:1.4.0
          resources:
            requests:
              cpu: "500m"
              memory: "512Mi"
scenes.narration: This deployment declares that three replicas of an ETL worker should always be running. The selector matches pods by their app label, and the template describes the pod that gets created, including the exact image version. The resource requests tell the scheduler how much CPU and memory each pod needs so it can place them on suitable nodes.

scenes.heading: Pod alone vs Deployment
scenes.narration: A bare pod has no safety net, so if it dies it simply stays dead and you scale it by hand. A deployment continuously reconciles toward a desired state, restarting failed pods and keeping the replica count steady. It also gives you rolling updates and easy rollbacks, which is why you almost never run bare pods in production.

scenes.text: Deployments manage pods, and Services expose them: declare the desired state and let Kubernetes reconcile.
scenes.narration: The mental model to keep is that deployments manage your pods while services expose them, and you simply declare the desired state and let Kubernetes reconcile reality toward it.
